key_insight: Modeling the dual roles of ‘creator’ and ‘editor’ enables a rigorous four-class detection that distinguishes pure human, pure LLM, human-created-but-LLM-edited, and LLM-created-but-human-edited text, revealing signals missed by standard binary/ternary detectors.
problem_solved: Existing detectors conflate different mixed-origin texts; the paper addresses the need for fine-grained identification of who authored vs who edited text to support nuanced regulation and policy decisions.
method: Define a rigorous four-class taxonomy (human, LLM, human→LLM edit, LLM→human edit) and curate evaluation data for these roles.
Develop a role-aware detection model that explicitly represents and disentangles creator vs editor signals to classify the four categories.
Design training objectives and evaluation metrics tailored to fine-grained detection and compare performance against binary/ternary baselines.
impact: Provides practitioners with a more actionable detection tool for moderation, provenance, and compliance by differentiating LLM polishing from human rewrites. This supports targeted policy responses and improved forensic analysis of generated text.
visual_elements: Taxonomy diagram showing the four-class split (human, LLM, human→LLM, LLM→human)
Schematic of the role-aware model (creator vs editor pathways) with brief annotations
Confusion-matrix or bar chart comparing binary/ternary vs four-class detection performance
Before/after text examples illustrating LLM polishing vs human rewriting
paper_title: Beyond the Final Actor: Modeling the Dual Roles of Creator and Editor for Fine-Grained LLM-Generated Text Detection
paper_authors: Yang Li, Qiang Sheng, Zhengjia Wang, Yehan Yang, Danding Wang
